subsubtopic: MEASURE TO PROTECT PRIVACY OF INDIVIDUALS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, as all those who have spoken on this bill since the beginning of the debate, I think individual freedom and protection of privacy are essential matters. We should ask ourselves the following question: will the bill now before us, namely bill C-25, truly contribute to ensure individual freedom and independence for all people in spite of the overwhelming bureaucracy and more particularly, data collecting agencies which are responsible for gathering personal information on individuals? It is clear that this bill means well, just as the road to hell is paved with good
June 2, 1977

intentions. It is an ambitious piece of legislation which aims at putting an end to all forms of discrimination through the appointment of a board and a tribunal on human rights.
These two bodies might become another administrative mess as well, bulging with ineffective officials trying to solve discrimination problems. Mr. Speaker, judging by the usual measures taken by this government, there is every reason to believe and especially to fear, that all this commission and this tribunal will do will be to reduce unemployment somewhat by providing good jobs at high salaries to a few cronies of the Liberal party. But, as I said, Mr. Speaker, it is possible, if not probable, that the government introduced this bill with the best intentions. For my part, I believe that we are once more on the wrong track with this kind of bill. It is not by setting up commissions, subcommissions and subcommittees that we are going to solve our problems. It is not either, Mr. Speaker, by lavishing money on problems that we will find answers. Before legislating to solve a problem, we should always ask ourselves whether legislation is a good means, an effective means of solving the problem. In the present case, the problem seems to be one of discrimination in all its aspects and of protection of privacy.
In fact, our interest in such problems is the economic implications of discrimination and violation of privacy. It is a fact that a person cannot get a particular job because of discrimination, or that an individual loses his job because of a report concerning his private life he was never informed of. In both instances, the individual that is economically dependent on the job he is seeking or the one he is losing is subjected to economic hardship by the unacceptable actions of his current or potential employer.
As I said, Mr. Speaker, the individual is victimized in that his economic position, his economic security are jeopardized by the unacceptable actions of some individual who is in a position to cause financial harm to those against whom he is prejudiced because of the colour of their skin or the length of their hair. As far as I am concerned, they are the victims of discrimination, and I suggest that above anything else they cry out for the protection of their dignity. And the best way to protect an individual's dignity is to put him in a position where he will not be dependent upon those who want to revile him. Whenever he is independent from those who would deprive him of his rights, he can protect himself against their scorn and unacceptable behaviour. If, on the other hand, he is dependent, because for instance he absolutely needs the job that is available, he is automatically in a dependent position. Mr. Speaker, the law can force an employer to hire an individual, but it cannot prevent the employer from despising that individual or hurting him with subtle harassment that affects him deep down.
The tribunal is not always aware of the facts. The commission will not always be in a position to assess the quality of the relationship between the employer and the employee. Consequently, the main effect of this well meaning legislation, as I
Canadian Human Rights
said a while ago, will be to place discrimination sufferers under the control of the individual whose only aim is to strike a blow at his dignity and integrity. Mr. Speaker, is that the purpose of this legislation? I am convinced it is not. We all wish to make discrimination impossible, because it affects the dignity of the individual. We suggest that a person can be protected against discrimination only if his economic interests are protected against those who try to discriminate against him. Mr. Speaker, we may wonder how it can be done. We feel that by ensuring the economic security of each person, we would ensure individual freedom for all. No person is free if he is financially dependent. If he must crawl on all fours to earn his living, he is not free, he is utterly at the mercy of the person who gives him a mere pittance.
That is why, Mr. Speaker, Socreds have been demanding for several years a guaranteed annual income for each and every citizen as a basic and unquestionable right. We regard the guaranteed annual income as the basis of individual freedom. A person who has a guaranteed income does not need to ingratiate himself with, or work for, an employer who despises or is prejudiced against him. How many times, Mr. Speaker, did our dear and sorely missed friend Real Caouette mention how undignified it was for people over 65 to have to beg for any kind of menial work, because the government would not support them, when they could have stayed at home with the guaranteed income we are proposing.
Mr. Speaker, of course the guaranteed income will only be possible if we agree to a fundamental restructuring of our present economic system. The reforms we advocate are an essential prerequisite in that regard. I am afraid that members of other parties do not give social credit principles and solutions the attention they deserve. It may be because they think they know them well enough already, or perhaps because they are satisfied with the present situation. Judging by what some government members are saying, I am afraid those were not and never will be understood. The fact that they are pressing for urgent measures to solve our economic problems is evidence to me that they are not satisfied with the present situation. On the other hand, their everyday attitude demonstrates that they know nothing about the principles and solutions advocated by our party.
It is impossible to understand Social Credit unless one accepts from the outset the fact that changes advocated by this party imply fundamental changes in our economic system. The reason is very simple: the defects of the present economic system are so deep that the only possible solution lies in rethinking and rebuilding the financial system on new bases by adopting new principles. If one wants to understand Social Credit, the most logical procedure is to consult the works of its founder, Major C. H. Douglas. In 1933, replying to two professors who were critical of his ideas, as are many members in this House towards Social Credit representatives, he stated in a few words what he found wrong with the current economic system, and I quote:
First of all, financial credit claims to be, but is not, a reflection of real credit. This means that our society's financial organization neglects true factors of production and consumption.

June 2, 1977
Canada Deposit Insurance Corporation Act
There is no logical and automatic relationship between, say, the capacity of the people to purchase goods and the capacity of the producing system to make them available.
That, the same Major Douglas used to say, is the main result of technological progress. Yet, we must admit that financial costs keep increasing, and this in spite of technological progress. It is therefore evident that the current financial system must distort reality. But let us push this line of reasoning a little further. It is generally recognized that we can improve our economic situation during any given period, that is to say our productivity is greater than what we are spending to market it. In other words, consumption is then only a fraction of production. Now, Mr. Speaker, if we want our economic system to reflect reality and if we accept the idea that the true cost of production is consumption, this means that if we want the public to have access to our production as a whole we must share among our people the purchasing power which represents the difference between what is consumed in the production process and the amount of production.
As for us, Mr. Speaker, we think that the guaranteed annual income we are proposing could be paid to every individual on the basis of this gap existing between the available production and the purchasing power now available to them. Accordingly, we would be better advised to try first of all to secure economic independence for every citizen, really without any discrimination, and give to every one regardless of colour, sex or hair length, a guaranteed annual income as a matter of basic right. So, Mr. Speaker, nobody would have, as it is proposed in this legislation, to work for an employer who could harass him because he is prejudiced against him.
The commission and the tribunal provided under this legislation will only be able to place an individual in a dependent position towards his employer by allowing him to work for someone capable of subtly torturing him by his scorn. Mr. Speaker, what I suggest and what we have always suggested is to allow the individual to be financially independent so he may have a decent life without having, in order to make both ends meet, to work for an employer seeking to humiliate him. This is, Mr. Speaker, a sensible position. This is a reasonable position. This is a proposition which could ensure respect for human dignity without going through the bureaucracy and the red tape which we will be facing when this bill is accepted at second reading. Then perhaps everybody, even some hon. members, may live to regret having endorsed the bill.

AMENDMENTS RESPECTING PREMIUMS, SHARE CAPITAL, ETC. The House proceeded to the consideration of Bill C-3, to amend the Canada Deposit Insurance Corporation Act, as reported (without amendment) from the Standing Committee on Finance, Trade and Economic Affairs.

speakeroldname: Hon. Donald S. Macdonald (Minister of Finance) moved:
speechtext:
That Bill C-3, an act to amend the Canada Deposit Insurance Corporation Act, be amended in clause 9, by striking out line 42 at page 6 and substituting the following therefor:
"a deposit.
(4)	Notwithstanding subsection (1), for the purposes of deposit insurance with the corporation, where moneys are received by a member institution on or after April 1, 1977, for which the member institution has issued or is obligated to issue an instrument of indebtedness other than a draft, certified draft or cheque, travelers' cheque, prepaid letter of credit or money order,
(a)	the moneys do not constitute a deposit unless the instrument and records of the member institution specify the person entitled, at the date of issue of the instrument, to the repayment of the moneys evidenced thereby;
(b)	the person referred to in paragraph (a) shall be deemed to be the depositor in respect of the moneys unless particulars of a transfer of the instrument are entered in the records of the member institution in which case the most recent transferee shown in the records shall be deemed to be the depositor; and
(c)	the entry of a transfer in the records of a member institution is ineffective, if the entry is made subsequent to the termination or cancellation of the deposit insurance of the member institution.
(5)	Notwithstanding subsection (1), moneys received by a member institution on or after January 1, 1977, for which the institution has issued or is obligated to issue an instrument of indebtedness other than a draft, certified draft or cheque, travellers' cheque, prepaid letter of credit or money order, do not constitute a deposit where the instrument is payable outside Canada or in a currency other than Canadian currency."
He said: Mr. Speaker, I wish to give just a few words of explanation about the amendment. The present definition of "deposits", as it is in the act now, broadly speaking includes all demand deposits in Canadian dollars and all term deposits having a maturity of five years or less. Term deposits in this sense would include guaranteed investment certificates issued by trust companies and debentures issued by mortgage loan companies. One of the changes proposed in the definition would withdraw deposit insurance from debentures or deposit receipts that are issued in bearer form.
Since insurance is limited to $20,000 per person per institution, it is essential that the deposits be in registered form in order that a determination may be made concerning the amount of deposit insurance. When the act was originally passed, this was not considered to be a problem, but in recent years there seems to have been some tendency toward the use of bearer-type instruments. A provision to this effect was included in the original terms of Bill C-3. However, as a result of scrutiny of the bill, by the financial community in particular, it became apparent that the provisions as put forward did not adequately meet the problems or the demands of the market. It was on the basis of this that a redraft was considered and the present amendment put forward.
One problem that has come to light is dealt with in subclause (5) of the amendment. Not only are we dealing here with bearer-type instruments but with the issue of instruments
June 2, 1977

to holders outside of Canada in currencies other than Canadian dollars. The amendment to the bill arose by reason of the floating of an issue of debentures in the European market, using as part of the sale's presentation the fact that the debentures, as issued, would be insured by the Canada Deposit Insurance Corporation. It was the view of the directors of the CDIC that the use of deposit insurance in this way was not in accordance with the general intention of deposit insurance and, consequently, this type of debt instrument should not, in the future, be eligible for deposit insurance.
The amendment, accordingly, proposed that instruments intended for sale abroad not be considered as representing a deposit, and also that bearer instruments not be considered as insured deposits. It was not intended to withdraw insurance from deposits made in Canada by non-residents. The revised wording has the advantage over the preceding wording, first, that questions of the validity of transfers of instruments are not raised. Instead, it is provided that an instrument does not represent an insured deposit unless the name of the payee is registered on the records of the issuing institution. As I indicated, the purpose was for clarification. There is a belief now in the financial community that this meets the requirement. As I said before, a number of the types of instruments issued in the manner in which they were issued went well beyond the original purpose of the deposit insurance. It is for this reason the limitation has been put forward.

Mr. Speaker, in replying to the statement of the minister with respect to his proposed amendment, I remind hon. members that this is actually the second version of the amendment that the Minister of Finance (Mr. Macdonald) has proposed with regard to this change. I would point out that when the committee reviewed Bill C-3 it was not asked to consider this amendment. There was no suggestion that there was a problem at the time the committee studied the bill. It is most unfortunate that this lack of foresight is so evident in so far as the government's actions are concerned.
It is not just the economy that the government is running poorly. They are running their own internal administration very poorly in the sense that they bring bills into this House, take them to committee, make no mention of further amendments, and by the time they get to report stage, with apparently no particular demand from any source they propose new amendments, then withdraw those amendments and give us an amendment such as we have today.
I was rather surprised to hear the minister say that the amendment in its present form is acceptable to the industry. That is not my understanding. Over the dinner-hour I am going to check with the president of the Trust Association in Canada to find out whether at the last minute he acceded to the suggestion the minister has made.
It is a fairly important amendment that we are considering. Through the innovation of certain trust companies and loan companies we have been able to win some foreign funds expressed in Canadian dollars for the benefit of those who need mortgage money in Canada. As we know, mortgage
Canada Deposit Insurance Corporation Act interest rates are unduly high in Canada. They are certainly unduly high compared to mortgage rates in many other countries. Our trust and loan companies have found there is a market for the sale of their debentures or guaranteed investment certificates in these foreign countries. Because they have shown that initiative, because they have been true entrepreneurs, the government steps in and says they do not want them to bring in these funds from foreign countries. The impact of this amendment is to make it difficult for the trust and loan companies to attract these funds and offer the general insurance provisions of the CDIC. We in the House must consider whether that is a wise move.
I hope the minister will respond to some questions later in the debate in order to give us some insight into why he and the Department of Finance believe we should accede to this request. Why are we making it more difficult to bring mortgage money into the country? That is the net impact of the amendment we are now considering.

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO CONVERT IAC INTO CHARTERED BANK
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should like to take a few minutes to conclude the remarks I made on May 5, remarks which meant to demonstrate that if we are serious in the House, we should, before we grant IAC its request, be able

to answer very precise questions on the grounds for granting this company its request. For instance, why does IAC want to become a chartered bank? Why should we grant it a charter and, if we do, why not grant similar powers in other areas, to ease the creation of credit?
Mr. Speaker, the answer is obvious: why does IAC want a charter? To make profits, but more easily than it does by lending real capital since, to lend real capital one has to have it, while banks, through their charter, can lend air, credit, and consequently, can lend figures; so, one readily understands that making profits out of nothing is interesting and consequently that is the goal IAC has set for itself.
One could ask: Why should IAC not be granted a charter when dozens of other financial institutions across the land are? To that I would say that I object to its request because it does not need a charter. Do we really need, at this point in time, more financial institutions to make things easier for the consumer where credit is concerned? No. I would go even further and say that, on the contrary, there are enough of them. One can then wonder whether a new bank is being created to give more services, with which I would agree; but I doubt that it is the case in this instance, and I proved it on May 5. On the other hand, if we agree to give that charter, we should take advantage of the situation to have a say about what is good for IAC shareholders.
Why should it not be good for the Canadian provinces also? Why, in other words, should the provinces not be able to turn to that possibility and create the credit they need and so achieve the progress that is essential to their development? Mr. Speaker, the question is quite simple, and we have been putting it to the House for years; but, unfortunately, it is a question to which we have been refused an adequate answer.
Of course the principle under which IAC could lend up to $16 million against a $1 million deposit is not bad in itself, if we have the potential. But in the current inflationary crisis where indeed we are witnessing a day-to-day price escalation the end of which is not in sight, we must wonder how long we can go on approving new financial institutions when the problem is the people's purchasing power. People have no real capacity either to buy what they need in everyday life, because the system has finally succeeded in creating all by itself a genuine inflation, or to sustain the level of production that may be needed.
If we in this House decided on granting what IAC wish, we would be inconsistent. We would solve none of our current problems, we would simply allow financiers to exploit the people still further by granting loans with rather high interests rates. To conclude, Mr. Speaker, I oppose the granting of a new charter to IAC, to the extent further that the same principle is disallowed when it comes to the government helping citizens achieve what would be needed for the progress of our country as a whole.
June 2, 1977

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO CONVERT IAC INTO CHARTERED BANK
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would like to express very briefly my views on second reading of Bill C-1001, concerning the corporation commonly known as I AC, which is requesting a bank charter under the corporate name of Continental Bank of Canada.
Mr. Speaker, I have often questioned in this House the principle of granting chartered banks the right to make money out of the nation's credit, to allow institutions to make profits by creating the deposits needed for private industry and even the government to make certain operations. Looking at statistics, we realize that the Canadian banking system is making profits while other segments of the economy are hard put to survive. We are even experiencing a high rate of bankruptcies by Canadians firms, headed by experienced people but not afforded the privileges granted to chartered banks. The right hon. Prime Minister himself (Mr. Trudeau), in an interview given to Fortune magazine, was emphatic about this, bitterly complaining about bankers.
Having said that both inflation and unemployment are high at the same time he asks: "What do bankers say to that?"
He was asked that question: What do they say? Here is his answer, Mr. Speaker, and I quote:
1 shall tell you what they say. They say that the federal government interferes too much in business, that the government must put an end to that policy, that that policy of interference is at the root of all our problems.
He added, and this is what I find unbelievable, Mr. Speaker, it expresses the conviction of the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) and it is the same conviction I want to express myself. He said this, and I quote:
"The worst grumblers . . .
What is a grumbler? It is somebody who has all the advantages possible and yet complains about the fact that others have some advantages. So he said this, and I quote:
"The worst grumblers are bankers. They have never had it so good since I am at the head of the government.
He rightly added, and I quote:
1 am ashamed. They make much more profits than the manufacturing sector, the natural resources sector and the service area as a whole.
They are at the top of the scale as regards profits. This is understandable. Mr. Speaker, if 1 enjoyed the same advantages, you can be sure that 1 would have at my disposal almost inexhaustible revenue sources which would enable me to be among those who make up what is known as the financial dictatorship. But as I do not have such means and I am in a position to realize they are in the hands of private institutions which compete with the state financial system, 1 believe it is my duty as a member of parliament to tell the House it is time for this situation to change.
Mr. Speaker, I am aware that the government has introduced legislation asking Parliament to postpone the introduction of a banking legislation which should normally expire in 1977, since under the law, the legislation concerning banking institutions and chartered banks must be reviewed every ten years, but as the years go by, this government, with the
Continental Bank of Canada
approval of chartered banks, is about to skip a decade. By continuously postponing reconsideration of legislation, we manage to delay and this year we are still delaying so that we might succeed in skipping a whole decade. But that is not the point.
The Canadian banking system goes back to 1817, according to some research I have made, when nine Montreal merchants went into partnership to carry banking operations. Similarly, two banks without statute began to operate in Lower Canada in 1818. The first to have a legal status was the Bank of New Brunswick, the smallest of the provinces in Confederation. Its incorporation was considered by the provincial legislature and received royal assent in 1820. The other three banks of Lower Canada did not get their charter before 1822. Other banks were established in the following years; most of them under provincial charters which tried to guarantee their stability and security. In 1850, an act which provided the free operation of banks in this province, inspired by the New York State legislation on the freedom of banks, was passed in the province of Canada.
Under that act individuals, alone ,or in partnership, and limited companies could set up banks if they had a minimum capital of $100,000. However, those banks could not have branches and their liability could not exceed three times the amount of the paid-in capital. Notes intended for circulation had to be obtained from the receiver general of the province and guaranteed by a deposit of an equivalent amount in government bonds. Those notes had to constitute a preferential debt on the liability of banks and were convertible on demand in gold. The act allowed any commercial bank which already had the right to issue notes to forgo that right in part or in its entirety. Those government notes were not subject to the 1 per cent tax set up in 1841 on bank notes in circulation.
Senior members in this House will remember seeing notes of different Canadian chartered banks. But after the Bank of Canada was set up in 1935, chartered bank notes gradually disappeared from circulation and were replaced by Bank of Canada notes. But the fact that chartered banks relinquished such privileges did not stop them from continuing to control and monetize the credit of the nation. So much so that in 1976, according to Statistics Canada, the money supply in Canada stood at $71 billion and was controlled in a proportion of up to $66 billion by chartered banks in Canada through the creation of deposits to make loans to institutions, businesses, or even governments either of Canada or the provinces.
Mr. Speaker, that provision regarding the multiplication of credit organized and allowed by the legislation provides that with a reserve of 8 per cent a bank may create deposits and lend money known as bank money. Under the law, that allows banks with, let us say 8 per cent reserves on which the bank pays interest, to create deposits and lend up to $100 to private borrowers, I think, or governments. If this is not a case of a government relinquishing its right to control the creation of currency under the form of credit, I wonder what it is. Mr. Speaker, I understand quite well that the fact that creating a bank or letting one disappear is not going to change anything
6230

June 2, 1977
Continental Bank of Canada
to the system, and when a corporation applies to become a chartered bank putting forth as an argument that this will enhance competition in Canada and in so doing lower interest rates, I do not believe it, because at one time we had 25 banks in Canada and competition was no fiercer than today.
These banks have merged over the years, with or without permission being granted by the Canadian government and we have reached a state when we now have only 10 chartered banks and the most recent one created by an act of Parliament, the Unity Bank, is in the process of merging with the Provincial Bank of Canada. Even if there were 12 or even 15 they will still have the same privileges of creating money for the purpose of making loans either to individuals or to the government, and that is precisely what is wrong with the system.
Mr. Speaker, chartered banks should be subject to the same legislation as savings or credit cooperatives, which cannot lend money by creating deposits and which must use deposits made by members of the institutions. It is this formula that we oppose, this generosity on the part of Parliament, this privilege for these new institutions, the issue of new bank charters to people or corporations wanting to become incorporated under the Bank Act.
I would like my contribution to be understood by all Canadians because I am convinced of one thing, and that is that if all Canadians were truly aware of the way in which our chartered banks operate because of legislation passed by Parliament, not many of them would approve of the monetary system of our country. The private monetary system is in the hands of the chartered banks, which control the money supply of the country and before whom the Canadian government has to go down on hands and knees to obtain the necessary credits to be able to face the many problems of our country. This is why we have inflation. This is why the government and the whole country are now facing serious unemployment. It is because money has become the monopoly of these institutions instead of the servant of the whole nation.
Even if I talked for one hour, I know that it would change nothing in the situation. I am aware of this, but at least I want to do my duty as a representative of the people and to make every effort to urge for a change of this situation. Nevertheless, 1 know that the majority will necessarily win eventually, but I will surely have the opportunity to speak again before the Committee on Finance, Trade and Economic Affairs if the bill is referred to this committee for future study, and we shall certainly then be able to suggest amendments so that at least the bill may correspond to the general legislation instead of providing for exceptions. Many clauses of this bill are in contradiction of the Bank of Canada Act.
We can see exceptions for this and that if at least we stick to the letter of the Bank of Canada Act and of the legislation requiring that a bank charter be given to some institutions or businesses in conformity with the present statute. In any case, I hope that in the next twelve months at least we will have the opportunity in the House to discuss in depth all this banking legislation, our monetary system and that, together, we will

endeavour to correct this whole system to serve the government and the whole nation so that instead of having a people prostrate before the dollar sign, we have a people which forces the dollar symbol to serve the nation.

The House resumed from Thursday, March 10, consideration of the motion of Mr. O'Connell that Bill S-2, respecting Bell Canada, be read the second time and referred to the Standing Committee on Transport and Communications.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Order, please. Before I recognize the hon. member for Timiskaming (Mr. Peters) again, may I inform him that he has already spoken for 17 minutes and has three minutes of his time left.

Mr. Speaker, I would have been more pleased if Your Honour had not told me how limited my time is; however, at least I know. When I spoke on March 10 of this year I said Bell Canada is hoodwinking us in its application with regard to its capital structure. Its relationships with its subscribers are not what they appear. The company is not operating, 1 suggest, only as a public utility. It has a monopoly hold on certain sectors of the economy and the activities of certain of its subsidiaries are highly questionable.
Bell Canada
I am pleased to note that by reason of government action, deliberate or otherwise, the CRTC, and not the Canadian Transport Commission, is to oversee the functioning of Bell Canada. By so doing the government made a wise choice. Although the commission has not looked into the question of stock relationships, it has criticized the company's operations, particularly the operations of certain subsidiary companies the operations of which it is difficult for the company's shareholders to control. Actually a large majority of the company's Canadian shareholders have all but lost the ability to control the operations of certain subsidiaries. The commission said that the company appeared to have made a profit of about 12 per cent, not the 7.8 per cent the CTC originally said was reasonable. It questioned the company's seeking some $3 million in advance payments or deposits from people it considered a poor credit risk.
When I last spoke on the bill I mentioned a small telephone company not far from Ottawa operating an exchange with 121 subscribers. By some strange quirk that small company controls a fleet of jet aircraft used by Bell Canada, controls Place Bell Canada, and prints telephone directories. At least it controls their printing. I think the directories are published by Tele-Direct.
The question is, how can such a small company control such large investments? The company operates a small telephone exchange serving 121 subscribers whose rates have not been increased for some time; so far as I know they will never be increased. How could a small company, serving a small number of subscribers, amass the capital with which to buy one jet costing between $5 million and $6 million, let alone a whole fleet of jets? How could it gain control of Place Bell Canada? I see that my time has almost ended, Mr. Speaker. I want to say much more. Perhaps I will be able to do so later this afternoon.

speechtext:
Deal with the amendment now.
80016-54(6

June 2, 1977
Bell Canada

-Bell Canada came to parliament and asked us to make a change in their relationship to their shareholders. In asking for time to allow them to reconsider the situation I think it would be wise for us to go back to see exactly what they did years ago.
Bell Canada was set up by the Canadian Transport Board in 1927, according to information which I received from Robert E. Babe, Ph.D., telecommunications economic consultant. The Board of Railway Commissioners, later called the Canadian Transport Commission, dealt with the first general rate case in 1919. The board held that the company should be permitted to earn profits sufficient to pay a $2 dividend per share plus "just and reasonable" retained earnings. This basic method of regulation continued in existence up to 1966. Bell paid a $2 dividend every year from 1891 until the mid-1950's, with the exception of the depression years.
In 1927, another rate increase was sought by Bell. The Board finally realized that the above procedures alone afforded very little protection to the subscribing public. While Bell was prevented from making excessive profits by regulation, the company was able to sell stock to existing shareholders at prices well below market value and pass on monopoly profits in the form of capital gains rather than income. However, since the new capital funds raised in this manner were insufficient to purchase assets that would yield the approved earnings per share, the company was able to argue in rate cases that it could no longer meet its dividend and permissible earnings per share under the existing rates.
The following quotation from the 1927 decision of the Board is instructive:
It was stated that it was not an unusual practice with prosperous companies. On this point it would seem proper to draw a distinction between a company engaged in competitive business and a company having a monopoly in operating a public utility. In the case of a competitive company the burden of its acts rests upon itself. But in the case of the company whose service is a monopoly and whose tolls are fixed or varied on the responsibility of public authority ... I am unable to concede that the company should be authorized to charge tolls which have in view the payment of an 8 per cent dividend on stock which did not realize for the company the increased assets that its actual value made available, to the amount of $3,529,217 on the $17,843,900 of stock which was sold to the shareholders at par in the years 1921 to 1925.
In 1929 parliament revised the Bell Act to require approval by the regulatory authority for all issues of stock.
Since 1929 the regulatory board has approved the issue price of Bell's stock and the company has been forced to sell its stock at prices above par, that is, $25. However, sales of stock at substantial discounts from market value have continued to be an important factor in Bell's financing down to the present, in spite of regulatory supervision. Note, for example, the decision of the Board of Transport Commissioners in 1966 at pages 658 and 688 where it is noted that new shares were sold to existing shareholders and employees at prices equal, on average, to 75 per cent of market value.
In pamphlet No. 16, 1966, of the judgments, orders, regulations and rulings of the Board of Transport Commissioners for Canada it is indicated that there is a cost saving to the company in issuing common stock only to shareholders and

employees, namely, the underwriting fee. This cost saving should be deducted from the difference between the issue price of shares and the market value of shares in order to estimate the net amount of stock dilution. In the 1975 issue of 5.2 million "units", comprised of one share in Northern Electric and one half warrant of Bell Canada, the issue price was $26.50, the underwriting fee was $1.25, and proceeds to Bell were $25.25 per unit. For exemple, the underwriters' fee was 4.72 per cent. This is a far cry from the average discount of 25 per cent given employees and shareholders. It is estimated that Bell lost about $166 million in capital through such stock dilutions, 27 per cent of capital raised through stock issues, over the period 1960-1971.
At the company's urging, the regulatory board revised the methodology of regulating the company in 1966, replacing control on earnings per share with percentage return on average total capital. This, to a substantial degree, has lessened the incentives of the company to water its stock.
Since the company is now allowed a percentage return on its book equity-book equity being net proceeds to the company from stock issues-the company has an incentive to inflate its rate base by issuing stock at as high a price as possible.
In the brief prepared by the consultant for the Consumers' Association he argued that earnings per share plus control over the issue price of equity is a much more effective way of regulating the company than the present percentage return on capital. If legislation is passed to prevent the regulatory body from authorizing the terms and conditions of new stock issues, a return to this effective method would be impossible.
What all this means is that Bell Canada has been playing around for a long time with issuing stock, and the method which it adopted mainly was a very simple business practice. Their criterion was not to try to serve the public as a public utility operating for the common good, or to try to satisfy the subscribers on the basis of the myth which they created that the company is controlled by several million Canadian shareholders, small people like the man who lives across the street from you, Mr. Speaker. They are basing it on the idea that the stock must carry a dividend sufficient to allow that little old widow, whom everyone knows but really has not seen for a long time, to live. Because of this they ask for such things as a 20-cent pay telephone charge.
I am pleased to see that the CRTC is not nearly as stupid as the Canadian Transport Commission has been over the years. The CTC has never found out why things are done. Perhaps even the CRTC would not have acted if it had not been for some bright newsman who pointed out that when you put a quarter into the slot to make a 20-cent call, you do not get a nickel back. Bell was stealing a million dollars from the Canadian public.
It is very interesting to read what the CRTC is reported to have said. It is rather complicated. It always is. The CRTC said that there is an inconsistency in the decision to charge 20 cents in some places, because in hospitals and certain other
June 2, 1977

insitutions the cost is ten cents. It is very difficult to justify why it is ten cents in hospitals but 20 cents in senior citizens homes and other places. The CRTC said it would get rid of this disparity by reducing the rate. That is the first time I have ever seen a government agency do that kind of thing. They usually get rid of disparity by raising rates, not lowering them.
The CRTC told Bell it could not charge 20 cents anywhere, that it would have to reduce the rate to a uniform ten cents. If the CTC, which deals with freight rates, had been dealing with these public telephone rates, it would have required everyone to pay 20 cents. It is interesting that up until recently the CTC adjudicated on these matters as well as freight rates. Even the government found that rather odd, so now we have the CRTC.
Nobody believes that pay telephones make money, but as a result of this reduction it is said that the loss to Bell will be about $9 million a year. The CRTC ruled that it is the responsibility of the telephone company to provide the public with convenient access to telephones at a wide variety of locations. All 20-cent telephones must be converted to ten-cent telephones within six months, and the commission is further undertaking to find out whether Bell has enough pay phones in service and, if it does not, where additional telephones are needed. CRTC looked into a number of other things. A lifeline service has been put into effect in a number of places. It looks as though the CRTC is doing something with this corporation.
However, considering what has been done with regard to Bell stock, considering the shocking way Bell has treated its common stockholders, and considering what Bell has done in terms of capital, which has affected very disproportionately the common and preferred shareholders of the company, I feel that it has not been managed responsibly. Bell has been able to tell the public to take or leave its service because it has a monopoly, and there is nothing the public can do about it. Certainly if there is any nationalization to be done in this country, the first company to be put on the list should be Bell Canada. I think everyone in the country would agree that if nationalization is justified in the public utility field, it is justified when it comes to telephone service.
I do not know how even the most unenlightened person could look at the assets of Bell and listen to the arguments which have been made before the commission without agreeing with me. Bell has indicated to the commission that it is not able to meet the basic requirements which have been established. One provision allows Bell to have a profit which would allow a $2 share dividend on common stock, and yet Bell has been able to buy an organization called Northern Electric. It has been able to buy Northern Telephone and a number of other small companies across the country.
Bell has established satellite control. It controls Capital Telephone, with its vast resources but no income at all. Bell has been able to do all this in the public field without being cited for stealing. Bell has not been cited for any of its other abuses. I suppose it would not be very difficult for a preferred shareholder or a common shareholder to lay charges against Bell under the normal procedure and to get some kind of redress for what has been done to him. However, if anybody
Adjournment Motion
had been at a commission hearing and seen the battery of lawyers retained by Bell Canada, he would know that in a life of 50 years or 60 years there would not be sufficient time to proceed with that type of action.
Now we are being asked to allow Bell to do a number of things it was not previously able to do. It seems to me that, before parliament makes these changes, this matter should go before the CRTC so that it could weigh all the "b.s." it has been handed with regard to Bell's rate structure and its financial background and ownership. Bell is having problems with deferred profits. It has been able to distribute those profits over the years, but it is now having difficulty with them because they fit into a capital gains position. There is a problem with regard to how to dispose of those deferred profits, but with people always coming into Bell Canada there will always be a disposition of those profits.
Northern Electric and Bell Canada have always been related as far as rates are concerned. Mr. Speaker, I see it is six o'clock, and I would like to continue this for several more hours, so I would like to call it six o'clock at this time.

subtopic: SPORTS-USE OF POST OFFICE FOR DELIVERY OF DEPARTMENTAL MAIL-MINISTER'S POSITION

speakeroldname: Mr. John C. Crosbie (St. John's West):
subtopic: SPORTS-USE OF POST OFFICE FOR DELIVERY OF DEPARTMENTAL MAIL-MINISTER'S POSITION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on Tuesday I asked a question of the Minister of State (Fitness and Amateur Sport) (Mrs. Campagnolo). I asked whether her department is no longer using the Post Office but, rather, using a courier service to deliver its mail. She said that to her knowledge it is not using a courier service but that if it ever does she would probably entertain the idea of using Newfoundland dogs. That was significant because she is not now using Newfoundland dogs; she is using a Newfoundland minister.
Last Friday the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Jamieson), the minister from Newfoundland, utilized a government jet at a cost presumably of approximately $3,000 or $4,000 to fly from Ottawa to St. John's, Newfoundland, to perform the ceremony of handing over a cheque to the Canada Summer Games Committee in St. John's. The ceremony took place at the airport. I have a picture of the minister in all his glory handing the cheque for $1.5 million over to the chairman

June 2, 1977
Adjournment Motion
of the summer games. The contribution of the federal government to the games is a paltry one, some $4 million in total; the province of Newfoundland is contributing over $5.5 million.
The minister took the cheque to Newfoundland by jet but, Mr. Speaker, the cheque could have been given to the members of the Canada Summer Games Committee when they visited Ottawa on May 16, or it could have been sent by registered mail for 20 cents or 30 cents. Either way would have saved the taxpayers of Canada several thousand dollars. Rather than that, however, the Secretary of State for External Affairs, who is supposed to be a busy minister, jetted to Newfoundland to present the $1.5 million cheque.
A newspaper report said that the minister stepped off the government "King Air" jet at Torbay airport, complimented the committee on what it was doing, and disclosed that the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) and the Governor General will officially open the games. He added that the games would be of enormous benefit to the province, jumped back in the plane, and took off for his riding where he spent two days politicking.
This is improper use and wasteful use of government funds. The minister could have travelled to Newfoundland first-class on Air Canada as he is entitled to, at a probable cost of $400, but instead he took the government jet at a cost of $3,000 or $4,000.
Questions have been put on the order paper about the minister's air travel. The hon. member for Leeds (Mr. Cossitt) set down Question No. 2,028 on March 7, and last December I set down a question inquiring about the minister's travels to Newfoundland in the jet last September in relation to a byelection to be held in October. Those questions have not been answered; the minister refuses to answer them. I would venture a guess that his travel bill exceeds that of the Minister of Transport (Mr. Lang) in the last two or three years. Neither of them wrote the book "The Fear of Flying". I would say that the Lang air service has now been out-paced by the Jamieson jet service or the Jamieson "air farce".
I ask the minister, or whoever is going to answer for him, to tell the House when the questions on the order paper will be answered. Perhaps the minister has lots of time now. We know that CIDA has been taken from him and given to the President of the Privy Council (Mr. MacEachen); we know that all negotiations with French-speaking countries have been turned over to the Minister of Supply and Services (Mr. Goyer). It reminds me of that old joke about putting your false leg in the corner and putting your false teeth in the glass. The minister will soon have nothing left to do. As I said yesterday, he will be the minister responsible for Saint Pierre and Miquelon if all his duties are given to other people. Perhaps he has nothing better to do than to fly back and forth to Newfoundland.
This silver tongued orator will find his tongue turning to gilt if he will not answer some of these questions. If the Secretary of State for External Affairs wants to jet to Newfoundland to present a cheque, or if the Minister of State (Fitness and Amateur Sport) wants to take a government jet to British Columbia to present a cheque, surely the public is entitled to

know the cost of this pandering to the wasteful habits of cabinet ministers.
In the old days there was a movie entitled "Flying Down to Rio", that has. been replaced by the picture of cabinet ministers thinking that they are emperors, flying about in jets no matter how lowly the mission-delivering cheques, delivering mail, picking up dogs, flying their nannies around. I think the public is entitled to know the cost of this arrogant behaviour.
I have a poem here in honour of the minister, which goes as follows:
You may fly free to St. John's
If you are a friend of Don's
If you think the cost too high
Don't cross Don's path in the sky
It is becoming positively dangerous to use the commercial airways because you never know when one of these ministers in their jets will be delivering a cheque to your area. I certainly do not want to get in the way when the Secretary of State for External Affairs has in his hot little hand a cheque for $1.5 million and is rushing to St. John's with it to have his picture taken.
I would ask the parliamentary secretary to answer question No. 2,028 set down on March 7 about the minister's travelling expenses in the last several years. On October 12, question No. 29 was put down by the hon. member for Leeds about the use of DOT aircraft. On October 12, question No. 30 was asked by the hon. member for Leeds with regard to the use of Department of National Defence aircraft by the minister.

subtopic: CANADIAN BROADCASTING CORPORATION-APPOINTMENT OF MR. O'NEIL TO HEAD PUBLIC AFFAIRS PROGRAMMING-POSSIBILITY OF MORE BALANCED PROGRAMMING
CANADIAN BROADCASTING CORPORATION-APPOINTMENT OF MR. O'NEIL TO HEAD PUBLIC AFFAIRS PROGRAMMING-POSSIBILITY OF MORE BALANCED PROGRAMMING
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on May 5 the Montreal Gazette carried an article with the headline "O'Neil to head TV public affairs". It reads in part:
The former press secretary to Prime Minister Trudeau has been appointed head of public affairs programming for the Radio-Canada television network.
Pierre O'Neil served Trudeau until September, 1975, when he went to the University of Dakar in Senegal to train French-language journalists. The date his new job begins has not been set because he is still in Africa.
That led me on May 17 to ask the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) the following question:
Adjournment Motion
I ask if, in making the personal appointment, the Prime Minister instructed the CBC to make a balanced presentation of public affairs and news programs in order to avoid those situations of which government members were so critical?
It strikes me first of all that the Prime Minister did not deny the purport of the questions, that is, that the appointment of Mr. O'Neil was a personal appointment to be a kind of a watchdog over CBC television programming. That is his specific duty.
This is to be seen against the backdrop of some outspoken statements by cabinet ministers. 1 have here some screaming headlines from the Toronto Star, for example, of February 23. In the article itself, the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce (Mr. Chretien) was reported as saying, "If you were to ask me if there were to be no CBC until after the referendum would I be more comfortable, I would say, yes." If that is not a kind of veiled blackmail, I don't know what it is. In effect the minister is saying, "Hey, if we can't get the CBC to perform the way we would like it to perform, we would be better off without a CBC."
The Minister of State for Urban Affairs (Mr. Ouellet) and the Minister of National Revenue (Miss Begin) have made similar outbursts. I ask you, Mr. Speaker, what would it be like to be a CBC reporter putting together a news broadcast or an editorial comment on the CBC presenting material which was mildly critical of the government? It seems to me we are developing a climate where everything is valid and objective only if it is in agreement with the government line. I do not know whether we ought to tolerate this.
The Minister of National Revenue, for example, is quoted in one article as saying that the CBC reflects separatism and nothing else. Another thing which strikes me as remarkable is that the premier of Quebec, a former colleague of the Prime Minister, was formerly an announcer and broadcaster for the CBC and nobody thought there was anything strange about this until after November 15 last. One of the cabinet ministers in Quebec had the most popular show in the province for months, even years, before her election. Nobody thought anything of it even though they knew she was a PQ partisan. That is the backdrop against which the Prime Minister's appointment must be seen.
I repeat: what must it be like to be a newscaster or an editorialist on the CBC today when all the time they are afraid that if they make a comment, or broadcast a news comment which is unfavourable to the government, they are likely to find one of the cabinet ministers bursting out in headlines in the next day's paper, saying, "This is not loyalty; they are not representing the government fairly."
The issue today is freedom for the public broadcasting system. Since the Prime Minister has made his own personal appointment to a very sensitive area of the programming department and of Radio Canada, 1 wonder whether Mr. O'Neil is not the watchdog, whether he has a red telephone to the Prime Minister's office over which he will be saying, "Look, there is something here which is not quite the way you would like it."

June 2, 1977
Adjournment Motion
The issue here is freedom, but it seems to me that the Prime Minister's interpretation of freedom in broadcasting is freedom for himself to regulate it and put his own man in place so that he can control the news coverage which emanates from the system. The power of the government is the power of appointment, and as long as the government exercises this power in such a partisan way, making sure that its own people are in these posts of great sensitivity, we shall find a government which is increasingly paranoid every time something is broadcast to which it takes exception.
I find it objectionable that the Prime Minister would make such a personal appointment in such a sensitive area in order, it would appear, to control the kind of news which comes out of the province of Quebec. I think it is time for the Prime Minister to become a little less sensitive about the kind of news broadcast in the province, and to preserve genuine freedom and objectivity, and thereby the unity of our nation.

speakeroldname: Mr. Jacques Guilbault (Parliamentary Secretary to Secretary of State):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Secretary of State of Canada
subtopic: CANADIAN BROADCASTING CORPORATION-APPOINTMENT OF MR. O'NEIL TO HEAD PUBLIC AFFAIRS PROGRAMMING-POSSIBILITY OF MORE BALANCED PROGRAMMING
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I find regrettable the attitude taken by my colleague for Surrey-White Rock (Mr. Friesen) of assuming that because Mr. O'Neil is a former press secretary of the right hon. Prime Minister of Canada (Mr. Trudeau) his nomination was decided by the Prime Minister, because this assumption is totally wrong. That nomination was decided by the CBC management, as it is supposed to be. Hon. members are well aware that the only positions in that corporation where candidates can be designated by the government are those at the upper management level, namely the members of the board of directors.
If you will allow me some comments on the choice made by the CBC, I will mention to you some information made available to me by that corporation; in addition to having been in the position that he is mostly known for, namely in the service of the Prime Minister of Canada, Mr. O'Neil has also been a correspondent of two newspapers, La Presse and Le Devoir, at the Quebec National Assembly as well as in the press gallery here in Ottawa. This man has therefore held some prestigious functions in the news-reporting business and has acquired a broad journalistic experience especially in the field of politics and government. One can therefore understand why the CBC chose to name a man of such experience to such a position, so the inferences made by my colleague from Surrey-White Rock are less understandable given the fact that the Prime Minister did not deny it lately. I can understand why the Prime Minister did not deny it for it is crystal clear that he was not the one who made that nomination.
Regarding the remarks made by my colleague concerning the balanced programming we should be getting from the CBC, I must tell him once again that we are dealing here with a mandate which is entirely placed under the jurisdiction of that corporation, and that neither the present government nor any other government of Canada can interfere in that respect because of the legal conditions that surround the creation of the CBC. And finally, let me add that if, on various occasions, some members of the present cabinet have raised their concern
[Mr. Friesen.)
about certain things they did not like with the CBC, this is precisely because the CBC is an independent body. If the government were in charge of the CBC programming, the ministers would have no reasons for disagreeing with the contents of certain programs simply because assuming the government were to control those programs, the corporation would have to go along with the views of the government. Mr. Speaker, I just wanted to set the facts in their true light and remind the House that this nomination stems from a decision made by the CBC management, as should be the case and as provided for by an act of Parliament, without undue interference on the part of the government.

subtopic: INCOME TAX-LEGALITY OF INCLUSION OF BENEFITS FROM LOW INTEREST LOANS AS INCOME FOR TAX PURPOSES
INCOME TAX-LEGALITY OF INCLUSION OF BENEFITS FROM LOW INTEREST LOANS AS INCOME FOR TAX PURPOSES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, this debate arises out of a question I put to the Minister of National Revenue (Miss Begin) on May 19 concerning the proposal which the minister announced to tax the benefit provided by low interest loans from employers to employees. I asked this question inasmuch as the courts, it seemed to me, had ruled that there was no necessity for anyone to charge interest at any specified rate, or indeed any rate or interest. The minister relied in her answer on section 6(1 )(a) of the Income Tax Act, which provides:
There shall be included in computing the income of a taxpayer for a taxation year as income from an office or employment such of the following amounts as are applicable:
(a) the value of board, lodging and other benefits of any kind whatever-
The provision then goes on to list some exceptions, which I should like to refer to later. The minister may have been correct in the narrow sense of the law, although she made reference in her answer to the spirit and the letter of the law.
I should point out that in 1956 the words "of any kind whatever" were added to that section or its predecessor section in the former Income Tax Act. That may have been because of an Appeal Board case in which the minister was seeking to tax interest to a shareholder, who may have also been an employee, because he borrowed money from the company in order to buy majority shareholders' interests. At any rate, it was held that no benefit was conferred on the appellant by the company in the years under question, 1952 and 1953. The exact words of the Appeal Board tribunal were:
Apart from specific legislation in a taxing statute, I know of no law which imposes an obligation upon a lender to demand the payment of interest in connection with a loan granted by the lender to a borrower, and if the lender does not require the payment of interest, the borrower is under no obligation to pay interest.
I would like to refer also to a case from the Exchequer Court, which was the forerunner of the Federal Court of Canada. In this case companies were being dealt with, but I think the principle is the same. This is the Pillsbury Holdings Limited case, and I would like to read from the summary as follows:
June 2, 1977

The amounts of interest so foregone by the subsidiary companies in favour of their parent company were construed by the minister as benefits conferred on a shareholder within the meaning of section 8(1 )(c),...
The taxpayer's appeal was allowed by the Tax Appeal Board, and the minister appealed to the Exchequer Court. The Exchequer Court held the following:
That a benefit received from a corporation by a shareholder must be received by him qua shareholder for the benefit to fall within section 8(1 )(c); a taxable benefit could not be imputed in respect of a bona fide transaction;
The fact that the interest was waived in this case was not held to be material and the minister's appeal was dismissed by the Exchequer Court.
The day before I asked the question, the minister responded to the hon. member for Edmonton West (Mr. Lambert) on a similar point. She said:
We have noticed a considerable increase in the loans, at low interest rates or without interest, being granted by employers to employees. We have therefore decided to revise our last interpretation bulletin to the effect that the difference between the interest rate on those loans and the bank rate will be considered as additional income, for income tax purposes, this ruling to become effective on January 1, 1978.
While it may be according to the letter of the law, there is certainly no equity involved in this. If it is the spirit of the law,
I doubt it very much because the government tells us that equity is the spirit of the income tax law.
Section 6(1 )(a) exempts any employer's contribution to or under a registered pension fund or plan, group sickness or accident insurance plan, private health services plan, supplementary unemployment benefit plan, deferred profit sharing plan or group term life insurance. If we are going to capture the benefit of so-called interest free or low interest loans from employers to employees, then I wonder when we shall be examining the matter of subsidized meals and employee discounts for retail outlets and that sort of thing.
Section 15 of the act allows a loan to shareholders, who are officers or employees of a company, without tax consequence if the loan is used for the purchase of a dwelling, to purchase treasury shares in the company, or to purchase an automobile to be used in the fulfilment of duties. It can also apply to a shareholder if the loan is repaid within one year.
We are creating a second class of taxpayers and further inequities by allowing deductions to certain classes of taxpayers, that is shareholders, and not to simple employees, and by legislating by the size of the loophole. The taxation of this so-called benefit was not thought of until it was realized that too many people were making use of it.

speakeroldname: Mr. George Baker (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of National Revenue):
speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
subtopic: INCOME TAX-LEGALITY OF INCLUSION OF BENEFITS FROM LOW INTEREST LOANS AS INCOME FOR TAX PURPOSES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the hon. member for Vancouver Quadra (Mr. Clarke) raised a question in the House of Commons on May 19, 1977, about a departmental interpretation that employees or shareholders borrowing money at less than a reasonable rate of interest receive a taxable benefit, and that commencing January 1, 1978, the value of the benefit will be computed as the amount by which the interest paid by the borrower is less than it would have been had a reasonable rate been charged. The hon. member referred to court rulings that
Canada Deposit Insurance Corporation Act there is no obligation for a lender to charge a specified rate of interest on loans, and asked how we would enforce such an interpretation without legislative approval. The Minister of National Revenue (Miss Begin) replied that there had been consultations with the Department of Justice respecting this matter.
The point is, Mr. Speaker that while it has been held that it is not obligatory for a lender to charge interest on a loan, in our view it does not necessarily follow that the borrower in these circumstances does not receive and enjoy a benefit. Such a benefit is taxable under the Income Tax Act.
In earlier years it was not a widespread practice for companies to make loans at low or zero interest rates to employees and shareholders, and where this was done relatively small amounts were involved. But the practice has grown over the years and in many instances substantially large sums of money are involved. The department feels it has a responsibility to check a practice that has clearly become an abuse.
Perhaps a simple example will suffice to illustrate how unfair it is to taxpayers generally when some taxpayers are able to enjoy the benefits of an interest free loan without incurring tax. Employee A accepts a $30,000 a year job. He buys a home, and out of his earnings pays $5,000 a year in mortgage interest. Employee B accepts a similar job for $25,000 but also receives an interest free loan from his employer that has enabled him to buy a home of the same value as Employee A's. Both employees would have $25,000 left, but under the practice that has been developing Employee A reports $30,000 of income whereas Employee B is taxed on only $25,000. The new interpretation has been issued in the interests of fairness and equity to all taxpayers.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, prior to the dinner hour I had been speaking on the amendment of the Minister of Finance (Mr. Macdonald) which is now before us with respect to Bill C-3. Perhaps I should read the portion of the amendment with which 1 want to deal. The amendment is in general reference to the activities of the Canada Deposit Insurance Corporation. Subclause (5) of the amendment reads:
Notwithstanding subsection (1), moneys received by a member institution on or after January 1, 1977, for which the institution has issued or is obligated to issue an instrument of indebtedness other than a draft, certified draft or cheque, travellers' cheque, prepaid letter of credit or money order do not constitute a deposit where the instrument is payable outside Canada or in a currency other than Canadian currency.
The reason that I read the subclause is that it will have two effects. One is that when an institution such as a trust or loan company takes a deposit that is payable in a foreign currency, it is not covered by CDIC. We do not object to that, that is fine, we are not suggesting that foreign currency obligations should carry in any way the insurance protection which CDIC is able to extend.
What we take exception to is that a Canadian dollar obligation, simply because it happens to be payable outside Canada, will not carry insurance protection. That is the effect of the subclause to which I have referred.
This amendment was triggered by the fact that Canada Trust placed a $25 million issue in Europe through a reputable investment house at 9.25 per cent, the issue being due December 31, 1981. Canada Trust did this in the latter part of last year. It was obviously a five year debenture which was placed by that underwriter with European investors. The interesting thing is that at the same time the Canada Permanent Mortgage Corporation placed the same amount, $25 million, at 9.75 per cent, with the same due date. In short, Canada Permanent did exactly the same thing. Its issue had the same due date, but Canada Permanent ended up paying .5 per cent more than did Canada Trust. Over the life of the debenture, that .5 per cent represents $625,000, so we are talking about a considerable saving, and I remind hon. members that that saving eventually accrues to mortgage holders in this country. That will mean cheaper mortgage financing for those who wish mortgage funds in Canada to the extent we can win cheaper foreign funds than are available in Canada.
The important question for us to consider is whether the department is correct in saying that that should be stopped, because frankly I do not think anybody in the CIDC had thought of it before. It was the innovation of the trust company to which I referred which triggered the department, and I think the department arbitrarily said that somehow it is wrong to have an issue like that placed in Europe with insurance attached to it. We say it is not wrong. What is wrong with getting cheaper mortgage money for Canadians?

If a trust company, loan company, or any other insured institution wishes to take in those funds anywhere in the world, as long as they are expressed in Canadian dollars what is wrong with winning those funds and hopefully getting cheaper mortgage rates for Canadians?
Prior to five o'clock the minister stated that he understood that the financial community was generally in agreement with the wording which we now have before us. Mr. Art Mingay, who happens to be the president of the Trust Companies Association of Canada says "No way". It comes as a great surprise to him that that representation should be put before us in this House. Incidentally, his company, Canada Trust, is the one I referred to when I referred to that $25 million issue.
Mr. Mingay feels that it would be preferable to refer this matter back to the committee and to allow the trust industry, perhaps the loan industry and other industries which are involved, to have an opportunity to explain why they feel that this is not a desirable thing to encourage as far as Canadians are concerned.
Our position on this amendment is that while certain parts of it-for example, the part which restricts the use of bearer certificates-are acceptable, we feel we cannot accept the suggestion that money which would result in lower mortgage rates for Canadians should be turned down arbitrarily just because a bureaucracy says it did not have that in mind at one point. There is no question that the insurance applies only up to $20,000. The issue which was placed in Europe is subject to that restriction. Those who are putting the money up in Europe, or wherever it is placed, are insured only up to $20,000 per depositor. Our suggestion is that the minister should reconsider this amendment and either withdraw it before the bill is passed this evening, or refer it back to the committee where that committee can have a second look at the bill with particular reference to the proposed amendment. Hopefully the amendment can be amended or withdrawn at that stage.
Do we in this House wish to encourage cheaper mortgage funds for Canadians, or, because the bureaucracy says it does not think that should be done, should we let the bureaucracy rule? Should we say, "To hell with the larger sector of the mortgage community; they can bear the heavy mortgage debt at higher rates; we feel that the bureaucracy must rule?"

He said: Mr. Speaker, as you pointed out so correctly, the purpose of the amendments standing in my name is to deal with the tax agreement with the Federal Republic of Germany. I should explain that since the tax agreement which is incorporated in the bill was negotiated between Canada and the Federal Republic of Germany, that country has brought in a new system of corporate taxation. For that reason it is the view of the Government of Canada that the tax agreement with that country should be renegotiated. On this basis we are asking parliament to delete all reference to West Germany from the bill so that we may go back and engage in these negotiations.
Under the old system in West Germany, undistributed profits were subjected to a corporate tax of 51 per cent while distributed profits were subjected only to 24.5 per cent. Under the new system the rate of corporate tax on undistributed profits is 56 per cent while the rate on distributed profits is 36 per cent. This, coupled with the 25 per cent witholding tax which is recognized in the new Canada-Germany tax treaty, would result in a substantial increase in the taxes paid by Canadian shareholders of German companies. The Canadian government therefore asked the German authorities for a revision of some of the provisions of the new agreement between the two countries.
The principal change in the agreement would be made in the dividend article; technical changes may also be made to other
[The Acting Speaker (Mr. Laniel).]
provisions of the agreement but they are expected to remain substantially the same.
I should tell the House that discussions with West Germany are scheduled for July in order to revise the agreement, and it is expected that the agreement will be resubmitted to parliament as soon as it is concluded.
I should also make reference to one minor amendment that is proposed to the treaty, and that is to correct an error that was made in the Canada-Morocco double-taxation convention. It is a typographical error in the Moroccan convention. On page 50 of Bill C-12 the cross-reference at the end of paragraph 2 of article 13 is to article 22, namely, the methods for prevention of the double-taxation article. It should instead refer to Article 21 which deals with taxation of capital. As I said, the error was incorporated in the original text which was signed between the parties. We have now received the agreement of the Moroccan authorities to make the appropriate convention in the treaty. The purpose of the amendment, therefore, is to reflect in this enabling bill the change that has been agreed to between the two sovereign states. This is the explanation of the changes put forward in my name.

speechtext:
motion No. 2:
That Bill C-12, An Act to implement an agreement between Canada and the Federal Republic of Germany and conventions between Canada and Morocco. Canada and Pakistan, Canada and Singapore, Canada and the Philippines, Canada and the Dominican Republic and Canada and Switzerland for the
