avoidance of double taxation with respect to income tax, be amended by deleting from the long title the words "and Canada and Switzerland".
He said: Mr. Speaker, I hope in the spirit of co-operation that is showing this evening that having acceded to the minister's motion No. 1 the minister will now accede to our motion No. 2 which we feel will have an identical effect to the minister's motion. He dealt with the treaty dealing with Germany. We are dealing with the Swiss treaty. We are simply suggesting that the Swiss treaty should also be deleted from the bill before us.
In dealing with the amendments I propose, 1 wish to point out that they are aimed at improving a bill which, with but one exception, is acceptable to us on this side of the House.
The general provisions of Bill C-12 respecting withholding taxes on dividends, interest, royalties and the like are, I believe, basically sound, and follow established international practice. Most members of the House would agree that mutual conventions of this sort are usually considered essential today in promoting the flow of trade and investment.
We have no objection to any of this. Our objections to this bill and the subsequent amendments arise in particular from the treaty with Switzerland and specifically from the provisions which ask us to confirm, under treaty, the privileged secrecy of those who would hide behind the secret numbered Swiss bank account.
Of all seven treaties-it is now six-embodied in this bill, the Swiss agreement is the only one to limit severely our access to information which would be vital in prosecuting tax frauds and other international cheats.
When we view it in comparison to concessions the Americans have won from the Swiss, the arrangements struck by our negotiators are sadly inadequate and do nothing to protect Canada from the numbered account type of dodge.
Following on the heels, as it does, of recent revelations that our own Crown corporations have been linked to unethical, and possibly illegal, payments into secret Swiss bank accounts, I find this treaty poorly conceived and ill-timed. It is a treaty which at this time defies common sense and the best interests of Canada.
1 would like to put on record four points which I urge hon. members to consider in the debate on this bill.
First, Switzerland is a tax haven. Despite the adamant insistence of the government in committee that Switzerland is not a tax haven because it levies taxes, a number of international financial experts think otherwise. One authority has this to say:
For more than a century Switzerland had been recognized as the most popular tax haven in Europe and the most stable on any continent ... In fact, surveys show that today Switzerland remains the leading tax-haven, next to Panama, in numbers of foreign based companies established in a single nation.
The source which gives several reasons for this, including low taxes, federal taxes on world-wide income begins at 3 per cent and graduates to 8 per cent, a hospitable climate for foreign investment and a unique banking system, is a publication entitled, appropriately enough, "Tax Havens of the

June 2, 1977
Income Tax
World" 1976 edition. If the minister is not familiar with that booklet, I am willing to send it to him so that there is no doubt in his mind as to whether Switzerland is in fact a tax haven. In fact it is the most sought after tax haven in the world, bar none. The fact that our negotiators are unable to identify a tax haven when they see one is reflected in the relatively weak safeguards embodied in this treaty we are asked to ratify.
Second, our negotiators have failed to gain concessions from the Swiss that were granted to the Americans as far back as 1951. U.S. officials, under a series of treaties with the Swiss, are able to obtain bank account balances, particulars of deposits, and even, in some instances, names of account holders when they are U.S. nationals suspected of tax fraud, forgery, or other criminal activity recognized by both countries. Swiss banking authorities have told me how naive they believe Canadian negotiators have been. Naturally, they speak off the record. But they say that compared to the negotiators from the United States our people literally did not know what they were doing when they sat down to hammer out this treaty.
The original 1951 U.S.-Switzerland treaty includes a phrase similar to ours limiting exchange of information, but with one major exception-Article XVI (1) incorporates a clause providing for the exchange of information "for the prevention of fraud and the like in relation to taxes which are the subject of the present convention."
The treaty before us may offer some little help in this regard but nothing so broad as is embodied in the U.S.-Swiss treaties which the Swiss Supreme Court has ruled can even take precedence over Swiss domestic laws of secrecy.
I would emphasize that our treaty contains specific words limiting our access to anything that is contrary to the laws of Switzerland. The contrast between our treaty and the American treaty is startling.
In the Prentice-Hall "Federal Tax Treaty Reporter" the following is stated in paragraph 82.014 regarding the case of X versus the Swiss Confederation Tax Administration:
Under Swiss Income Tax Treaties Swiss authorities could provide the Internal Revenue Service with data from records of a U.S. citizen's bank account when that citizen was charged with tax fraud, a crime in both countries, substantiated by the IRS and generally confirmed by investigation. Bank secrecy could be lifted for fraud as distinguished from mere assessment.
I suggest there is nothing in the Swiss treaty placed before us today which would give us anywhere near the kind of advantage the Americans have gained in lifting the veil of secrecy from those who would defraud their government. 1 might add that the Swiss are the first to state that they wish they could change the American treaty. They acknowledge the Americans have negotiated a tough deal. But, surely, Canadians can be equally tough-or, if they are not, we must draw other inferences from the fact that they have concluded an agreement with the Swiss as favourable as the one before us tonight.
As late as last August the Americans ratified a judicial and administrative mutual assistance treaty which provides for the

exchange of certified bank records, expert testimony and other assistance necessary for the prosecution of mutually recognized crimes. That treaty went into effect in January of this year, yet the government is proposing ratification of a treaty with Switzerland which falls far short of these conventions. It is inconceivable to me that we would not insist on similar concessions from a tax-haven country, especially in the light of the recent revelations which have been debated in the House and to which my colleagues will be referring later in the debate tonight.
We have little to gain from ratifying this treaty at this time and much to gain from waiting. Highly placed sources within the Swiss banking community have indicated that Swiss authorities are alarmed by certain defalcations in their banking community which have arisen from the use of secret accounts. Apparently only a few officials at any time-usually two-are allowed access to banking records and the government is unhappy about the lack of control over secret bank accounts. The Swiss, I understand, are themselves considering a crackdown on non-disclosure practices in that country.
Similarly, other nations, including the United States, are reportedly pressing for more open disclosure practices. These nations are urging the adoption of an OECD model agreement in the hope it would lead to better international co-operation in taxation administration and the prevention of fraud.
Why are we rushing into this treaty at a time when the Swiss themselves are questioning secrecy? In what way does this anxiety to sign a treaty with Switzerland to assist tax dodgers, with their secret accounts and a kind of pay-off system, tie in with the government's attitude toward Polysar? We have to ask some of these pertinent questions before voting one way or the other on this important bill. In short, why are we rushing into this treaty? A reform of the Swiss secret account system might yield, at another time, a more beneficial treaty for Canada.
The Swiss government itself is pushing for amendments to the treaty which is now before us. This was not made clear during the committee sessions. It has not been made clear by the minister to date. The treaty we are being asked to ratify tonight has, in fact, been partially amended, certainly in the initial sense, by the Swiss and the Canadian authorities. The reason we do not have the amended form before us tonight is that the government apparently intends to give effect to the amendments by order in council at a later date. It is interesting that these amendments should have been prompted by Swiss banks which were balking at certain provisions in the treaty which they felt could create an administrative nightmare for them.
In short, while the treaty goes far further than the Swiss would normally have expected, it goes far further than the United States treaty in terms of ensuring the secrecy to which I have been referring. On the other hand the Swiss bankers have said that it is too complicated, from an administrative point of view, and they hope to have those complications removed. We understand the Canadian authorities have hastened to assure them that this will be done on the assumption

Mr. Speaker, I should like to participate briefly in this debate in order to endorse strongly the position taken by the hon. member for York-Simcoe (Mr. Stevens) and to raise with the minister some concerns and apprehensions I feel might arise by virtue of accepting this part of the bill relating to the Swiss treaty, at the present time.
The point has been well made by my colleague from York-Simcoe that there is a distinction in the wording with respect to exchange of information. The identical provisions are not in the treaty with West Germany as are contained in the treaty with Switzerland. The minister may want to discount those particular words referred to by my colleague by simply saying they are merely an administrative provision. 1 would suggest to him that he look at the provision more closely in light of the well-known provisions in Switzerland relating to secrecy in bank accounts.
There has been considerable discussion in this parliament on the use of Swiss numbered bank accounts with respect to payments made by Crown corporations. That was referred to by my colleague from York-Simcoe. At the present time the Swiss are reviewing the whole question of their numbered accounts. I mention this fact because, in dealing with the observations and criticism raised by my colleague from York-Simcoe, it is my understanding that in Switzerland secrecy rules are not waived with respect to bank accounts. In criminal investigations tax evasion is not an offence in Switzerland. This is a very important point for us to consider in this debate.
On the basis of my reading of Article XXV of the treaty, any information we may want to get in Canada with respect to moneys going into numbered Swiss bank accounts, by virtue of an attempt to avoid the payment of taxes in Canada, does not necessarily have to be provided by Swiss officials. They do not have to provide that information to us under the terms of this particular agreement.

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO IMPLEMENT AGREEMENTS BETWEEN CANADA AND CERTAIN COUNTRIES TO AVOID DOUBLE TAXATION
speechtext: In fact it is a criminal offence for them to do it.

speechtext:
As the hon. member for York-Simcoe should know, the Swiss officials are now in the process of reviewing the whole question of Swiss bank accounts and are trying to set down a new code of ethics and a new set of rules with respect to numbered bank accounts. An attempt is going to be made to bring them under stricter control with a new agreement between the National Bank of Switzerland and the Bankers' Association.
Professor Leo Schuermann, the director general of the Swiss National Bank, said:
... the agreement will "settle to an important extent" the issuance of numbered accounts in Swiss banks-a special service long offered to assure anonymity.
Income Tax
The director general may be attempting to establish a new set of rules with respect to Swiss bank accounts. They have good intentions in Switzerland. I do not doubt that at all. As has been suggested by the hon. member for York-Simcoe, the acceptance of this treaty in its present form is somewhat premature, especially when we consider the fact that Swiss bank accounts are a very important element with respect to the whole question of double taxation and taxation matters in general.
The whole question of Swiss bank accounts has come under considerable pressure in Switzerland. They are pushing for reform as a result of a banking scandal last month at the Chiasso branch of Credit Suisse, one of the country's three largest banks. Losses from the scandal apparently involved an unauthorized flight of capital from neighbouring Italy, which is estimated at something like $400 million. One can understand that there is great concern with respect to that kind of flight of capital and funds into Switzerland.
The Swiss have their own reasons for wanting to improve and revise their own system with respect to numbered bank accounts and the secrecy provisions. These provisions have been in effect since the thirties. They were as a result of deposits of money from Germany, by Jewish and other German citizens, during that period of time. At that time Swiss banks facilitated the flight of money from Germany. The removal of money from Germany, prior to the second world war, was a capital offence. That is the genesis of the establishment of anonymous numbered accounts.
As I have said, pressure is developing because of the suggestion that since the Second World War secrecy and numbered accounts have led to repeated clashes between Switzerland and other western countries which have claimed that Swiss bank accounts have facilitated the flight of hundreds of billions of dollars to that country, largely to avoid taxes. That is the whole point of this particular treaty.
For the minister to stand up and suggest the provisions of Article XXV are clear and unequivocal, with respect to this very important factor, is premature on his part. That particular factor has been brought out clearly by my colleague from York-Simcoe. As he showed, some serious questions concerning this treaty need to be answered. We should not ratify the treaty until the Swiss have revised their own rules governing numbered bank accounts.
The government seeks to ratify this treaty after certain developments have taken place concerning government agencies. Those developments were reported by the media. The minister himself has had experience of and contact with Polysar, one of the Crown corporations now in the news.

A Crown corporation for which the federal government is responsible was involved in the payment of funds into a numbered Swiss bank account. What was their purpose? Such information has not been forthcoming. 1 suggest there is a distinct relationship between that activity on the part of an agency of the federal government and our sanctioning this treaty at this time. I say this in view of the language of the treaty, or in view of the language of Article XXV concerning the obtaining of information from Swiss authorities on taxation matters and information relating to collection of taxes from Canadian citizens, corporations and nationals.
I understand that in Switzerland tax evasion is not an offence. Perhaps the minister can verify this. In other words, if taxes are evaded in Canada, or if Canadian taxes are evaded, that is not an offence in Switzerland, and they would not be obliged to give us information. If we try to collect taxes from people using a numbered Swiss bank account, we shall be whistling in the dark, for they could use a numbered Swiss bank account in order to hide money taken from Canada illegally.
The minister is responsible to this House. He ought to review the position and consider again the ratification of this treaty. He should accept the eminently sensible advice of the hon. member for York-Simcoe and accept his proposed amendment. After all, we can still consider the treaty. Apparently the Swiss will begin reviewing their numbered bank account system on June 6, or in four days. I suggest we should not pass this particular part of the bill. Perhaps this treaty could be introduced in a separate bill, once the points raised by my colleague from York-Simcoe have been met. We could do it after the Swiss have reviewed the operation of numbered, anonymous Swiss bank accounts. I say this because we may find, even after the Swiss have enacted a new code of rules governing their numbered accounts, that the code is still not satisfactory.
We may want to change the language of Article XXV to provide for carte blanche exchange of information without qualification. The minister may want to seek a legal opinion on the effect of such a provision. Perhaps we shall need to renegotiate the treaty, but I think the Swiss authorities will be receptive to this idea, if my colleague for York-Simcoe is right; since he is right 99.9 per cent of the time, I am sure he is right this time. Actually, I think he was wrong only once, and that's so long ago that it is most difficult to remember the event.

1 do not think I make an unreasonable request. I suggest the Government of Canada should consider the consequences of ratifying a treaty imperfect in form, of perpetuating unsatisfactory conditions, and of countenancing the possibility of further incidents similar to the two or three raised not long ago in this House. I am talking of incidents involving Crown Corporations either directly or indirectly under the control of this government. I plead with the minister to reconsider the wording of Article XXV, to bear in mind the review which will soon begin in Switzerland, and to adopt the amendment proposed by my colleague from York-Simcoe.

Mr. Speaker, I note that the Minister of Finance (Mr. Macdonald) is still working on about 36 treaties. It seems to me that at the end of the month they will be about 18 months behind schedule. Speaking on the amendment proposed by the hon. member for York-Simcoe (Mr. Stevens) the minister commented on tax treaties, suggesting that we like to enter into tax treaties with co-operating countries. That is true in some cases. However, in other cases as in the case we are considering, the minister does not distinguish between countries which co-operate with Canada and countries which do not.
I wish to put on record some incidents concerning our dealings with Swiss enterprises, to show why the House should support my colleague's amendment. I suggest most hon. members remember that a Canadian Crown corporation, Atomic Energy of Canada Limited, paid $2.5 million U.S. as its part of the fee due with respect to the sale of a reactor. The money was paid to Intercontinental General Trading Company, a nominee of Banca Della Svizzera Italiana, Lugano, Switzerland. We could trace the money that far. Many attempts were made to trace the money further. All attempts to discover the destination of these funds were met with silence on the part of Swiss banks, although Swiss officials were fully co-operative.
I shall read some letters into the record. The first letter was written by the treasurer of Atomic Energy of Canada Limited to the head office of the Royal Bank of Canada, in Ottawa, dated December 14, 1976. It reads in part:

I am sorry to put all that material before the House, but I think the story has to be set out in a little detail so that we can understand the significance of the extended absences and of the spurious agreement to give further information which may be lawfully given to any properly constituted authority. Of course the answer that comes to us loud and clear is that it is not lawful under any circumstances to give any further or meaningful information.
The media were not entirely satisfied with the progress that was made by the Canadian parliament and its committees, and they made some attempts themselves in that direction in a recent story which, I believe, appeared in the Financial Post. The following paragraph was contained in the newspaper which indicated that the Swiss officials were at least in some way concerned. It stated:
Meanwhile, in Lugano, the public prosecutor for the Sottoceneri region of southern Switzerland confirmed he has opened an official investigation into AECL's payment of the $2.5 million secret commission to I.G.T., the Banca Svizzera Italiana (B.S.I.) nominee company. Nothing ever came of that investigation and no further information was ever made available to the Canadian parliament of its committee.
One might consider that that would be regarded as an isolated instance, but of course members of the House will also be aware of the fact that there was another Canadian involvement in the way of Polysar Limited, a Crown Corporation, and further millions of taxpayers' dollars were paid into numbered Swiss bank accounts. The fact that they are numbered may not be completely significant because I understand all accounts are numbered, but the point is that these were secret accounts.
Polysar, in the light of these transactions, as a Canadian Crown corporation stood accused of involving itself in procedures which could have had the effect of hiding tax revenues from the Canadian taxation authorities. These practices would have enabled foreign customers to avoid foreign exchange regulations in the countries where they were located. They could have had the effect of evading income taxes in the countries involved, and they could have had the effect of defrauding minority shareholders in the customer companies.
Many officials from the companies came and testified, and others were invited to come and lend their testimony to try to sort out this matter for the benefit of the taxpayers of Canada whose many millions of dollars had been involved in these practices. However, we found that many witnesses, first of all out of fear of the Swiss secrecy laws and Swiss laws which

prohibit disclosure of any information on the basis of confidentiality, refused to appear at all, and finally, on the assurance of the committee that no proceedings would be initiated against them for what they said here, they still feared their prosecution under Swiss law and said they would only appear if they were allowed to appear with Swiss counsel at their side so that they could be advised before they answered.
1 think my colleague, the hon. member for Saskatoon-Big-gar (Mr. Hnatyshyn), made reference to the banking reform that is taking place now in Switzerland in light of certain irregularities that have been discovered in the banking industry there. It seems that his plea that we wait until this reform is completed is a good one.
I would like also to refer to Article XXV in the treaty. I think the hon. member for York-Simcoe already referred to this. We find that in the Swiss treaty, unlike many of the others which we are being asked to pass at the same time, there is a strange reference to the exchange of information, and referring to this exchange of information the following clause is added: "being information which is at their disposal under their respective taxation laws in the normal course of administration".
It is difficult to understand that the minister was unable to explain what purpose this clause had in this particular agreement when it did not apply to the agreements of any other countries. And when one puts together the fact that Swiss law prohibits the release of information concerning bank accounts to any other competent authority, including the Government of Canada, and the fact that Swiss law would therefore not permit any information to be exchanged because it would not be at Switzerland's disposal as required under that clause, this can hardly be considered as the action of a co-operative and friendly government. I think the minister is not doing service to the House or to the Canadian taxpayer by rushing this bill through without considering these very important factors.
The minister well knows-and his colleagues can certainly remind him-of the furore which was created over the apparent careless use of millions of taxpayers' dollars in the instances to which I have referred.
For all these reasons I want to give my full support to the amendment proposed by the hon. member for York-Simcoe. It is certainly an unusual and unlikely event to see the Minister of Finance (Mr. Macdonald) here today equating himself with Swiss gnomes. He is the most unlikely Swiss gnome I have ever seen, at least here in this House, but tonight he aligned himself with the Swiss. When I refer to Swiss gnomes, 1 refer to financial gnomes. Why is Canada rushing to engage in a tax treaty with Switzerland? If there is any need to engage in a tax treaty with Switzerland, obviously we should try to get something out of it which is to our benefit. Other countries besides Switzerland are used by financial dodgers, financial skimmers, financial scallywags, financial carpetbaggers, financial birds of prey, or financial flim-flam men as places to take their ill-gotten gains and bury them in unnumbered, numbered, or unknown bank accounts.
If we are going to have a tax treaty with Switzerland, would that not be an opportunity for us to try to get some concessions from Switzerland so that our government will no longer have the excuse, when a matter comes up before the Public Accounts Committee regarding pay-offs to agents or whatever it is, of saying that it cannot get information on that matter, so that our government would be in a position to get information when information is needed for tax purposes or for criminal prosecutions, and so that the government can get information from Switzerland?
The government's absolute lack of action and lack of enthusiasm about doing anything to get some information for the Public Accounts Committee on what happened in connection with AECL and the pay-offs which occurred with reference to the Korean contract, and the pay-offs which occurred with reference to other contracts with Polysar, have been the most laughable things I have noticed in my brief months in this House. The government has had an absolute lack of vim, vigour or enthusiasm in attempting to get information on those matters. It is laughable that the government should absolutely accept the statements made by the people involved, who said that if they were to give information to the Public Accounts Committee they would violate the laws of Switzerland or some other country. They said they positively could not be expected to inform one of our House committees of the facts in connection with these pay-offs made by Crown corporations to agents, customers, or otherwise.
Frankly I am fed up with this. If Canada is going to enter into a treaty with Switzerland, with Panama, with Costa Rica, or with Liechtenstein, Canada should be getting something in return, and Canada should take some action to stop these countries from being havens for birds of prey who use them as places to transfer their ill-gotten gains, in a manner unknown to their own jurisdictions.

Let me give the House an example. We all know about the Churchill Forest Industries incident in Manitoba and about how an entrepreneur from outside the country was able to sweep into Manitoba, inveigle the govern-
June 2, 1977

ment into participating in the Churchill Forest Industries complex there, make millions of dollars, take them out of the country, hide them in Switzerland and in other countries around the world, and get away with it. That person still has not been brought to justice.
In Newfoundland we had a similar experience. When we came into office in Newfoundland in 1972 we came across a situation in which one John C. Doyle, a promoter for Canadian Javelin Limited, was involved in a matter with the previous government. The premier of the province, (Mr. Smallwood)-I think it was in 1965-gave a company known as Society Trans-shipping Incorporated of Liechtenstein-another tax dodge haven and another refuge for the criminal element of the world-a letter which said that company had the right to cut wood in 10,000 square miles of the mainland of Newfoundland, Labrador.
There was no order in council, no Crown lease, no Crown grant, and no document approved by the cabinet, but there was a letter from the premier of the province to Society Trans-shipping Incorporated telling that company it had the right to cut in 10,000 square miles, which I believe is bigger than the whole province of Prince Edward Island. There are 110,000 square miles in Labrador. Society Trans-shipping Incorporated of Liechtenstein, which had a bank account in Switzerland, sold its letter to Canadian Javelin Limited for $3.9 million. I am using round figures, but it was in that area.
Any lawyer who ever graduated from law school in this dominion could have advised Canadian Javelin Limited that the letter was not worth the paper on which it was written, that it did not have a scrap of legal validity, and that Society Trans-shipping Incorporated had not a jot or tittle of a right to do what it did. In fact even a layman could have advised that. Anyone but a numbskull, nitwit, or crook could have advised that that letter gave nothing. It certainly gave nothing worth $3.9 million belonging to private shareholders. That scrap of paper was signed by a premier and was authorized by a government, but there was no order in council and no legislation passed to validate it.
The question is: who owns Society Trans-shipping? That is the $3,900,000 question. Although I know who owns it 1 cannot prove it, nor can the Newfoundland government prove it, because no one can get behind the laws of Liechtenstein to find out who owns it. Are we putting up with this in Canada? We have no power in connection with Liechtenstein, but if a treaty ever comes before this House in connection with anything in Liechtenstein I will be 100 per cent against it until the Minister of Finance can find out from that country who is behind Society Trans-shipping and similar enterprises. That is the same sort of thing the government should be looking for in connection with Switzerland.
I happen to know that the $3,900,000 or whatever got transferred to Society Trans-shipping, went to Liechtenstein and passed through that country like a thief in the night to a bank in Switzerland. We can only guess where it went from

There seems to be a theme which has pervaded the remarks of members on this side of the House in our contribution to the debate. It is a theme I would like to endorse and speak briefly upon. It refefs to the question of openness, especially in matters of finance, particularly as they relate to government.
Since the tragic occurrence in the United States known as Watergate, there has evolved abroad in this land a cynicism about public life which is very discouraging to one of that generation that now forms over 50 per cent of the Canadian population.
When I was first elected to the House of Commons in 1972, I was asked, I guess because I was much younger in those days, to speak at a great many high schools in my constituency and in other places. Very often the first question put to me by students in assembly was: how does one go about getting elected to the House of Commons? At that time students were very excited about public life, interested in its challenges, and thought it to be a worthy pursuit.
A /ew weeks ago I spoke at two high schools in Hamilton. That question, which had not been posed for some time, was turned around and asked in reverse. I asked the students assembled if any of them would like to serve in public life at the municipal, provincial, or federal level of government. In the first high school I could not find one student who wanted to pursue a career in public life. At the second high school I found one student who thought he might take a chance in seeking public office.
I believe the reason for this change in such a short number of years in the attitude of Canadians generally, but especially young Canadians, about public life and a career in politics, has to do with the central theme to which I am referring-honesty and openness in politics, in business, and in our general approach in our everyday dealings with one another.
On the international scene relations between countries are really no different because countries are no more than a collection of individuals. Obviously we have different feelings toward different individuals, and countries have different feel-
Income Tax
ings toward one another. In all of those relations, be they interpersonal on a one-to-one basis, or be they in the international field of economics or politics, there should be certain constant principles. Foremost among them would be that of honesty.
The question facing us tonight is not only what benefit would accrue to Canada and the Canadian people by this bill sponsored by the Minister of Finance. Behind that we should approach it with these questions: does it promote honesty in our relations with other countries? Does it help promote honesty in the business of politics? Does it encourage a belief that there is honesty in international finance, honesty in diplomacy, and honesty and openness in public life?
Regretfully I must conclude, buttressed by members of the Conservative party who have spoken tonight, that the answer to these questions would be no. Rather than open up these central questions in a way that would encourage Canadians to believe that there is a new spirit of honesty in our approaches to international financing and politics, it does the reverse. It covers up. At a time when we most need openness and honesty, it is doing the exact opposite to what we need. That is deeply regrettable.
Mention has been made of Swiss bank accounts. As the hon. member for Dauphin noted, the Swiss authorities themselves are questioning the age old practice of having secret numbered bank accounts in Switzerland. Those of us who sat in the House throughout the scandal related to the payments made to a person or persons unknown using such bank accounts must be especially concerned as to what this legislation will do. It may encourage such practices to continue. I hope not. If that is the case, it is doubly regrettable, and surely no hon. member here would wish to see it passed.
I wish to congratulate those who have put forward in greater detail our reasons for opposing this proposition put before us by the Minister of Finance. I hope he will take our comments to heart, bearing in mind that it is not a case of opposition for personal reasons-during the debate several kind things have been said about him and if he does not find them encouraging he must certainly find them refreshing coming, as they do, from this side of the House. I endorse the remarks made by hon. friends because if we lose the interest of young Canadians in public life because we fail to pursue actively policies of openness in all our dealings at every level, nationally and internationally, there is no future for this country and no future for this institution, because politics will be lost by default, and those with higher aspirations will have lost faith in us. This may appear to be a supplementary issue, but I state it, to use a phrase often employed by another member of this House, with all the sincerity and conviction I can command as being a deep concern of mine.
I hope the minister and his officials, should this bill go forward, given the majority situation in which the government temporarily finds itself, will take these views into account and reconsider the action to which they have committed them-

Mr. Speaker, on behalf of my colleague, the hon. member for Edmonton West (Mr. Lambert), I should like to speak to his suggested amendment; the hon. member cannot be in the House this evening. I draw the minister's attention to the fact that at the first meeting of the Standing Committee on Finance, Trade and Economic Affairs held on November 2, 1976, the amendment before the House was substantially discussed, and at that time the minister's parliamentary secretary attempted to satisfy the committee with regard to the point.
In short, the amendment arises from the uncertainty which seems to exist in regard to the impact of the amendment that is in Bill C-8 itself. Hon. members who have read the bill know that the government is asking that the Financial Administration Act be amended in order to give greater facility for the signing of various discharges and other types of releases. My colleague from Edmonton West raised the point that he felt
June 2, 1977

that it had not been clearly defined exactly what the impact would be of these instruments and releases or discharges, whatever you like to call them. The suggestion was then raised that it would be better simply to refer to the instrument as being included within the definition which is found in clause 2(1 )(d) of the Statutory Instruments Act. That act was assented to on May 19, 1971. It appears as chapter 38 in the Statutes of Canada for 1970, 1971 and 1972.
For those who are interested, the subsection my colleague has referred to in his amendment is found at page 2 of the act. It is quite a lengthy description, but essentially it clarifies what a statutory instrument is. The thrust of the amendment before us is that, for clarification, the amendment the government is seeking should be added to with the view that it will be clear that an instrument of release or discharge shall be deemed to be a statutory instrument within the meaning of clause 2(1 )(d) of the Statutory Instruments Act.
To summarize, I am simply saying we are hoping the minister will accede to this request. It will clarify what we are seeking here in the main amendment which is found in Bill C-8. For greater certainty people would turn to section 2(1 )(d) of the Statutory Instruments Act to see what a statutory instrument will include. This point was raised at committee because the government seemed to be very casual in indicating what the releases for the discharges would be for which it was seeking the new found power to give. It stated that it was casual stuff which involved the Department of Indian Affairs and Northern Development, and sometimes mortgages were required to be discharged and other instruments of that type. We are fearful the amendment may be intended to cover that type of thing, but it will be interpreted in a much larger sense in due course. We will find releases and discharges may be given in a rather casual way, as a result of the amendment which the government is proposing, much more casual than is the case of such releases or discharges clearly defined as statutory instruments.
Statutory instruments, of course, would be reviewable by the Standing Committee on Regulations and Other Statutory Instruments. It is a proper safeguard for the Parliament of Canada through that committee to have a look at what exactly are the releases and the discharges which are being signed by ministers of the Crown. In truth, it is a tremendous power to be giving to a minister-the right of the minister to sign on behalf of the Government of Canada rights which otherwise might be accruing to the Government of Canada. Why not define it as a statutory instrument so that we have the protection of that act and the reviewability of each of the releases and the discharges before the Standing Committee on Regulations and Other Statutory Instruments which is contemplated?
In order to expedite matters tonight, that is as far as I should go. It would be interesting for members to hear the minister explain why he will either accept our amendment, or if not, why he decides to turn down this clarification we are seeking.

speakeroldname: Hon. Donald S. Macdonald (Minister of Finance):
subtopic: FINANCIAL ADMINISTRATION ACT AND SATISFIED SECURITIES ACT
subsubtopic: MEASURE TO REPEAL SECURITIES ACT AND AMEND ADMINISTRATION ACT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, what we are dealing with here, in the very simplest terms, is the present provision of the Satisfied Securities Act which requires an order in council and a cabinet decision about each discharge of a mortgage-or a lien of some kind taken by the Crown under one of the many statutes which provide financial assistance to various kinds of Canadians. At present the law requires that each one be as a result of a specific decision by cabinet or by a cabinet committee. For a better sense of administration, this responsibility should be transferred from the cabinet level to the ministerial level. This makes good sense in terms of administration. We are talking about the hundreds of thousands of instruments which are delivered every year under the Veterans Land Act and under the various kinds of statutes for which my colleague, the Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development (Mr. Allmand) is responsible. It does not make much sense to have this procedure dealt with at the cabinet level. It is a ministerial decision.
I have some difficulty understanding why the hon. member for Edmonton West (Mr. Lambert) would want to have the committee look at thousands of chattel mortgage discharges or lien discharges. It is not the kind of statutory instrument with which the committee was set up to deal. One might almost say that to include this provision, to encourage the committee to look at thousands of such documents every year, is a Machiavellian way of occupying the committee's time and therefore render it less able to concentrate on more fundamental matters.
There are two reasons for not accepting the amendment, and the first is purely practical and sensible. If you are talking about discharging mortgages, you are not talking about lawmaking statutory instruments. Indeed it is fair to say that we are not talking about statutory instruments at all. The relevant characteristic of a statutory instrument is as follows. I quote from the Statutory Instruments Act, that act cited by the hon. member for York-Simcoe (Mr. Stevens). It is that it is made "by or under an act of parliament by or under which such instrument is expressly authorized to be issued, made or established otherwise than by the conferring on any person or body of powers or functions in relation to a matter to which such instrument relates." It is my view that the proposed section 95.1 of the Financial Administration Act does not result in the creation of a statutory instrument to be issued, made or established but rather confers a power on an appropriate minister to execute and deliver an instrument.
As I say, it is somewhat hard to see the relevance of the issue. The only significance flowing from the fact that an instrument is a statutory instrument would be that pursuant to Section 26 of the Statutory Instruments Act it would stand referred to the statutory instruments committee. I am advised that the practice at the moment is that none of the instruments currently made by order in council pursuant to the Satisfied Securities Act is being referred to that committee. These documents are not required to be published in the Canada Gazette; therefore the position has been taken that they should

He said: Mr. Speaker, I am very pleased to introduce this bill for third reading. It was introduced last December, it has been reviewed in detail in the Standing Committee on Miscellaneous Estimates, and it has been the subject of discussion with the university community. I might say that I appreciate very much the co-operation I have had from both sides of the House in proceeding with the bill. I would just like to make some comments on this final stage of the bill.
The main impact of this bill will be on the university community. I believe the reorganization of the granting councils will open the way to a new relationship between the government and universities in research matters. Perhaps I might speak about that for a moment.
The growth of university research over the last 15 years or so has been considerable. In 1961-62 the granting councils provided $26.5 million to the universities; in 1977-78 the estimates for the councils call for $172 million to be spent on research grants.
In the rapid development of the universities in the 1960's, there was strong competition among the universities to gain recognition and status in research. Universities vied with one another in trying to build up schools of graduate studies very
June 2, 1977

quickly. I think it is fair to say that most of them had had little experience in guiding efforts in research, and few had a conscious policy which gave direction to these efforts. The emphasis was on attracting individual researchers of great ability who were then supported in research of their own choosing. Our universities, and Canada as a whole, benefited by bringing into their ranks scientists and scholars of outstanding calibre.
On the other hand, a price was paid. In nearly every university there are some well developed programs of research in certain departments, but generally there is a wide dispersion of research competence spread thinly over most disciplines. One would have to say this has been a consequence of the laissez faire attitude of both the universities and the granting councils to research growth. We cannot be too surprised at this. Priorities for research have not been clearly enunciated by government or the universities, and the councils, reflecting the prevailing view, have judged research or scholarly projects almost entirely on the competence of the applicant and on the scientific feasibility of the project. There has been little, if any, co-ordination of university research objectives regionally or nationally.
Since becoming minister of science last September I have visited many universities and talked to many university scientists and scholars in an attempt to understand what the role of university research should be. Is the main purpose of this role to push back the frontiers of knowledge? Is it to train graduate students to be competent researchers? Should it be helping to solve problems posed to it by governments or industry? These are difficult questions because universities are complex institutions serving many goals and constituencies of our society, but I believe the answer is all three. My perception is, however, that there has been an imbalance in favour of the first two and at the expense of the third. I have reached the conclusion that the universities must begin moving more of their research and inquiry into the mainstream of effort aimed at understanding and solving our pressing national problems.
I am not saying by this that research which is stimulated solely by the imagination of the researcher and whose objective is discovery, nothing more, should not be supported or should
Scientific Activities of Government be downgraded in any way. Curiosity-oriented research-or discovery oriented, as John Polanyi has said-must continue to receive solid support. Although the last few years have been tough, I believe that an even more selective process is needed, however, which will allow those relatively few individuals whose research is of recognized quality, at least nationally and possibly internationally, and who have shown a rare blend of knowledge, imagination and passionate interest in discovery, to be supported well, perhaps better than they have been in the past.
There are, on the other hand, many individual researchers and groups of researchers whose talents and dedication might equally be challenged by identifiable issues of priority concern to governments and the public at large. It has become apparent to me in my visits that the nature of the research enterprise in universities has been changing. The existence of cross-disciplinary groups-in environmental and policy institutes, for example-and the collaboration that has been taking place on large projects is shifting the attitudes of university researchers. Whether recognized or not, the laissez faire attitude to the support of university research has a much narrower validity than it once had.
What this means is that the time has come for a more activist approach by the granting councils to the determination of research priorities and to the creation of new policies and programs which will give university research an even greater opportunity to respond to national needs. Bill C-26 is important because it creates a new and dynamic framework in which this vital, evolutionary change in the direction of councils can take place.
I disagree wholeheartedly with an hon. member opposite who, quoting a university person, said in the committee "This bill represents an idea whose time has come and gone". I believe its time is very much now. Mr. Speaker, I see that you are agitated.
